title: Are there people who can't feel pain?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain congenital insensitivity to pain with anhydrosis (CIPA), a rare hereditary condition in which people cannot feel pain or temperature and cannot sweat. They cover how pain normally works (nociceptors, nerves, fear conditioning), the case of Dr. Geoffrey Woods and a boy in Pakistan, the history of the condition (first described 1847, discredited 1960s psychological theory), the suspected genetics (TRKA/NTRK1 gene, autosomal recessive, higher rates among cousin marriages), and dangers such as infections, overheating, self-injury, unnoticed fractures, and Charcot joints. Also covers parenting tips, a few support websites and a documentary, and a listener email from Ignacio about surviving the 2010 Chile earthquake and tsunami while listening to the podcast. Includes a brief ad read at the start and a correction segment at the end.

Stuff You Missed in History Class

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts joke around, mention Josh's shaved head, and introduce the topic of people who cannot feel physical pain.

segments.title: Defining CIPA and the Geoffrey Woods case
segments.summary: Introduce CIPA with anhydrosis as a subtype of hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy, with about 60 reported cases worldwide. Dr. Geoffrey Woods heard of a Pakistani boy who showed no pain, but the boy died around age 14 before the visit; the family was found to have similar insensitivity. Analgesia is noted as the term.

segments.title: How the nervous system senses pain
segments.summary: Explanation of pain signaling through peripheral nerves, spinal cord and brain, and nociceptors responding to mechanical, electrical, thermal and chemical stimuli. Pain is protective and linked to fear learning through direct conditioning.

segments.title: Causes of CIPA, anhydrosis and sweating
segments.summary: Different CIPA cases involve missing nociceptors, nerves not conducting, or lack of innervation. Anhydrosis means sweat glands are not innervated, so the body cannot cool by sweating, making overheating and infant death risks. Hosts joke about sweating personally.

segments.title: History and genetics of CIPA
segments.summary: First described in 1847; a 1960 psychological-cause hypothesis was discarded. A 1950s patient underwent painful tests without anesthetic. Genetics suggests a TRKA/NTRK1 mutation affecting nerve growth factor, and the condition appears autosomal recessive, with higher rates among related parents.

segments.title: Anesthesia history tangent
segments.summary: Brief tangent comparing insensitivity to ether-induced insensitivity, citing Dr. Crawford Long in New York City.

segments.title: Dangers and problems for children with CIPA
segments.summary: Children may not cry after injuries, leading to unnoticed infections, sepsis and fever. They may chew through lips and tongues, scratch eyes, forget to eat or use the bathroom, suffer unnoticed fractures, and develop Charcot joints. Parents may remove baby teeth or use goggles.

segments.title: Parenting tips, exercise, and treatment
segments.summary: Advice includes baby-proofing, checking children for injuries several times a day, moving to cooler climates, occupational therapy, and swimming for exercise while avoiding overheating. No cure exists; stem cell therapy is speculated as a future option.

segments.title: Resources and further reading
segments.summary: Hosts recommend the Gift of Pain website, a site about a boy with CIPA, and the documentary A Life Without Pain by Melody Guild, and suggest searching CIPA on the site.

segments.title: Listener mail: Chile earthquake and corrections
segments.summary: Listener Ignacio writes that he was in Chile during the 2010 earthquake and tsunami and listened to the podcast to cope. The hosts discuss the Day's Army family, then correct the pronunciation of De Pue (Illinois) and Yorba-type Canadian bacon jokes, and sign off with the email address.
